topic: Open Doc: The Document Framework Built for AI Agents
summary: open-doc (@open-document/core) is a React-first, agent-native document framework: the agent writes documents as React components, and the framework supplies A4/B4/A3 page geometry, self-filling contents and page numbers, DOM-measured auto-pagination, layout diagnostics the agent can read, and headless PDF/HTML/PNG/SVG export. It is a real but very early project — MIT, created 2026-08-17, 78 GitHub stars, 7 forks, 487 npm downloads/month for core, a single human contributor (LiuYuWei, 12 commits), last release 2026-09-03 (core 0.6.0 / mcp 0.3.2). Its differentiator is not the renderer (browser print pipeline, same as print-to-PDF) but the agent loop: skills that ship with the scaffolder (/create-doc, /doc-authoring, /current-doc, /apply-comments), an MCP server with 23 tools that shares one implementation with the browser UI, optimistic-concurrency text writes that refuse stale edits with 409, and `open-doc check`, which reports clipped content / stranded headings / unloaded images at source line:column so a blind agent can fix its own layout. The timing is notable: MCP's 2026-07-28 revision made the protocol stateless (no initialize handshake, no Mcp-Session-Id), which is exactly the shape open-doc's endpoint claims support for. The honest framing for the article: this is a well-argued new entrant whose ideas are more mature than its adoption, with the usual early-stage holes (no .docx export, an open allowedHosts/403 bug, no Letter/A5 support by design).
verdict: Promising, correctly-scoped, pre-traction. Ideas: strong. Ecosystem: ~500 downloads/month. Not yet a safe default for a team that needs Word output or a hosted service.
key_facts: Positioning: 'The document framework built for agents' — the agent writes React, the framework owns page geometry, outline, contents, page numbers, print layout and export.

Authored medium is TSX: one document = docs/<id>/index.tsx exporting `meta` (DocMeta) plus a non-empty default array of DocPage entries (fixed pages) and/or flow(<>) sections the framework paginates by measuring the real DOM.
Explicit self-comparison: 'If open-slide is Google Slides for agents, open-doc is Google Docs' — a deck is a 1920x1080 canvas, a document is a stack of A4 sheets that has to survive a printer.

Page sizes are deliberately restricted to A4, JIS B4 and A3, portrait or landscape (six sheets). 0.4.0 removed A4/Letter/A5/Legal; rationale is every sheet maps to paper a given print shop actually sells.
A4 is 794 x 1123 px @ 96 dpi, and the @page descriptor matches, so nothing is rescaled at print time.
MCP: 23 tools over stateless Streamable HTTP at http://localhost:5273/mcp, mounted by `open-doc dev --mcp`; no session handshake; legacy: 'stateless' serves 2025-era clients from the same endpoint.
Tools and browser share one implementation, so write_document / write_text take the content you last read (`expected`) and refuse a stale write with 409 instead of clobbering a concurrent human edit.

Agent-facing diagnostics: `open-doc check` renders every page at true size and reports content clipped past the sheet, blank sheets, headings stranded at a page foot, print-too-small type and images that failed to load — each with the source line:column — and exits non-zero, so it doubles as a CI gate.

Skills ship inside the scaffolder: /create-doc (asks four scoping questions, establishes source material first and 'will not invent your numbers'), /doc-authoring (technical reference), /current-doc (resolves 'this page' via node_modules/.open-doc/current.json), /apply-comments, /create-theme.

Long-form furniture resolves itself: <Footnote> prints on whichever page its marker landed on and its height is taken out of that page's budget before the packer breaks the page; <Ref> renders 'Figure 3' and adds '(p. 12)' only for cross-sheet targets; <ListOfFigures /> / <ListOfTables /> build the lists.
DataTable reads .csv/.tsv at build time into arrays of objects, so table numbers stay synchronous with the prose around them; numeric columns right-align with tabular-nums unprompted.

Export: PDF (browser print pipeline at true page size), HTML (self-contained, zipped when the doc has assets), per-page PNG and SVG. Headless export needs an optional peer dependency: playwright + chromium. No .docx.

Markdown in: `open-doc import notes.md --id q3-notes --contents` produces a real document (flow() body, cover, self-filling contents, GFM tables, local images copied into the doc's assets/) that is ordinary authored TSX.
Deploy shape: `open-doc build` emits a plain static site (Vercel / Cloudflare Pages / Netlify / any static host); `pnpm dev` runs a studio at :5273.

MCP security posture: Host and Origin are validated against loopback (blocking DNS-rebinding onto a local endpoint), both rejections are 403; nothing authenticates the caller, so anything beyond loopback needs an authenticating reverse proxy.

Monorepo: pnpm + Turbo, packages/core, packages/cli, packages/mcp, apps/demo (dogfood target). The repo also carries .agents/skills (doc-runtime-patterns, print-layout-review, viewer-ui-guidelines) mirroring .claude/skills.
Author/publisher context: the maintainer is LiuYuWei; the GitHub org path is simonliu-ai-product and the product page lives at costaffs.app/tools/open-doc/ — a CoStaff tool, not a standalone company.

competitors.name: open-doc (the subject itself — primary source)
key_points: README is unusually specific about the agent-blindness problem: 'An agent writing React has no idea whether the paragraph it just added pushed the last three lines off the sheet.'

`open-doc check` sample output documents the failure taxonomy verbatim: p.4 content runs 37px past the sheet and is clipped in the PDF; p.7 image failed to load; p.6 heading ends the page; each with a p: / h2: line:column locator.
Auto-pagination contract: `export default [Cover, Contents, flow(<>, { footer: Footer })] satisfies DocEntry[];` — headings never end a page, captions stay with figures, tables move whole.

Inspect mode edits text through AST replacement into docs/<id>/index.tsx, checked against what was on screen; mixed content splits into one field per text run so inline markup survives; notes persist as @doc-comment markers for a later /apply-comments pass.
Themes are documentation, not code: themes/<id>.md is a house style (palette, type scale, paste-ready components) with an optional <id>.demo.tsx for the gallery; meta.theme back-links the document.

Hard authoring rules stated to the agent: one index.tsx plus assets/, no sibling .tsx, no new dependencies, only react + @open-document/core + standard web APIs, do not touch package.json or open-doc.config.ts.

competitors.name: open-slide — the sibling idea in the deck medium (8,587 stars, MIT, created 2026-04-26, pushed 2026-09-28)
key_points: Same author-side philosophy and the same skill pattern (/create-slide with four scoping questions, /slide-authoring as the technical reference, @slide-comment markers + /apply-comments).
Fixed 1920x1080 canvas; pages are arbitrary React components, not a DSL.
Exports static HTML, print-ready PDF, and an editable PPTX where each page becomes native text boxes, shapes and images — done entirely in the browser, no server and no headless browser.
Has a presenter mode (speaker notes, timer) and svgl logo search integrated into the assets panel.

Vercel OSS Program badge; ~110x open-doc's stars. Key contrast: decks have one canvas, documents have a paginated paper contract — which is why open-doc needs a layout checker and open-slide does not.

competitors.name: react-pdf / @react-pdf/renderer — the incumbent for 'React to PDF' (16,813 stars, MIT, created 2016-10-18)
key_points: The default answer for programmatic React PDF and the scale comparison that matters: 22,574,136 npm downloads last month vs open-doc core's 487.

Different bet: it is a renderer with its own layout engine and a PDF-specific component set (Document/Page/View/Text), not a document workspace with skills, viewer, inspector, MCP endpoint and themes.
It can emit a real .docx-adjacent workflow's missing piece? No — it emits PDF only; it does not give an agent a feedback loop about clipped content.
For a writer: react-pdf is what you reach for when a service must produce PDFs at scale inside an existing app; open-doc is what you reach for when a person and an agent co-author a printable report.

competitors.name: Typst — markup-based typesetting (56,342 stars, Apache-2.0, Rust, created 2019-09-24)
key_points: The strongest 'agent can actually write this' alternative after Markdown: a terse markup language designed to replace LaTeX, with fast incremental compilation.
open-doc's counter-argument is that agents write prose well and markup badly, and that React is a medium the model already has deep priors for.
Typst's counter-argument to open-doc is determinism: a compiler has no browser print pipeline, no fonts race, no @page descriptor dropped by Chromium.
npm `typst` wrapper: 12,920 downloads last month — 26x open-doc's core.

competitors.name: Pandoc + Quarto — markup to output-format converters (46,452 stars GPL-2.0 created 2010; Quarto 6,032 stars, pushed 2026-09-28)
key_points: Pandoc: 'universal markup converter' — the 16-year-old default for Markdown to everything, including a real .docx that reviewers can track-change (exactly the gap open-doc issue #35 asks for).
Quarto builds a scientific/technical publishing system on Pandoc with an agent-friendly plain-text source and a real pagination story for books and reports.
These win on output-format breadth (docx, LaTeX, EPUB, ODT) and lose on layout feedback: none of them can tell an agent 'the table on page 7 overflows by 40px'.
npm `pandoc` wrapper: 6,780 downloads last month.

competitors.name: WeasyPrint — HTML/CSS to PDF (9,649 stars, BSD-3-Clause, created 2011-08-09)
key_points: The classic HTML-to-print engine with real support for the paged-media CSS model (named pages, running elements, widows/orphans).
Closest conceptual match to open-doc's page-geometry argument, but driven from server-side HTML/CSS rather than from a live, hot-reloading browser document a person and an agent share.
No agent tools, no viewer, no inspector, no conflict-checked text writes.
npm `weasyprint` wrapper: 1,419 downloads last month.

competitors.name: Sundial — agent-native document editor (HN, 2026-06-19)
key_points: Announced on HN as an 'Agent-Native Document Editor' (3 points — the whole niche is still tiny).
Represents the other architectural bet: a document editor/repo designed around agents, rather than a React runtime plus print pipeline.
Useful in the article as evidence that the category is being named and contested in 2026 by several small projects at once, not invented by one README.

competitors.name: OpenDoc (RyanYahya) — near-identical pitch, 2 stars (MIT, created 2026-09-12)
key_points: 'An open-source document production framework for beautiful, consistent PDFs and presentations with any agent.'

Created 12 days after open-doc went public and effectively a name collision — worth one line in the article as a 'check which OpenDoc you found' warning, since search intent for 'open doc' is already fragmented.

Also note the unrelated, much older open-doc projects in other domains (e.g. opendoc.dev-style names time out / do not resolve; the GitHub search for 'open doc' is dominated by this repo at 78 stars and a 147-star unrelated SQL repo).

competitors.name: MarkItDown — the inverse pipeline (187,655 stars, MIT, created 2024-11-13)
key_points: The most popular 'document + agents' repo by an order of magnitude, and it runs the other direction: files and office documents into Markdown an agent can read.
Pairs with open-doc in a real workflow: MarkItDown ingests the inputs, the agent reasons, open-doc emits the printable artifact.
Good for the article's framing that 'agent documents' is two problems — ingestion and production — and open-doc only solves production.

competitors.name: MCP 2026-07-28 revision — the protocol context that makes this design possible
key_points: Removed protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header; list endpoints no longer vary per-connection (SEP-2567).

Made MCP stateless: removed the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake. Every request carries protocol version and client capabilities in _meta (SEP-2575) — exactly the shape open-doc's stateless endpoint assumes.

Added a mandatory server/discover RPC so clients can pick a version up front, and multi round-trip requests (MRTR, SEP-2322) where servers return resultType: 'input_required' plus inputRequests instead of pushing server-initiated requests.

Removed SSE stream resumability and Last-Event-ID: a broken stream loses the in-flight request and clients MUST re-issue with a new request id — relevant when an agent's long `render_page` call dies mid-render.

Minor changes that bite local tool servers: required Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers on Streamable HTTP POSTs, ttlMs + cacheScope on list results (SEP-2549), deterministic tools/list ordering for prompt-cache hits, resource-not-found -32002 -> -32602.
Prior revisions a reader may still be running: 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26, 2024-11-05.

competitors.name: costaffs.app/tools/open-doc — the product/marketing page (and its staleness)
key_points: Frames the value in the operator's words: 'An agent hands you a block of Markdown; you need a file you can send to someone. The layout layer in between is not something you can dictate through chat.'
Four pillars stated on the page: PAPER (prints the way it looks), NUMBERING (contents renumbers itself), PAGINATION (tables never split in half), CHECKS (tells you what broke and where).
The page advertises 'v0.3.0 is on npm' while npm's latest core is 0.6.0 — the marketing page lags the packages by three minor versions, a concrete sign of how small the operation is.
Three-step onboarding on the page: npx @open-document/cli init my-docs -> /create-doc prompt -> open-doc export --pdf.

angles: The reframe nobody states plainly: agents don't produce bad documents, they produce documents with no layout feedback. open-doc's real product is the feedback loop (check -> line:column -> fix), not the renderer.

'Google Docs for agents': take the open-slide analogy seriously and test it — decks have one canvas, documents have a paginated paper contract, which is exactly why pagination and diagnostics exist here and not there.

React is a medium, not a format: why a model's deep priors on React beat a bespoke document DSL, and where that bet breaks (you inherit a browser print pipeline and its @page quirks — see the landscape descriptor bug fixed in 0.4.0).

Print fidelity as a first-class constraint: restricting the page-size set to A4/JIS B4/A3 x portrait/landscape is a product decision, not an omission — 'a document always maps onto paper someone can actually buy.'

Concurrency between a person and an agent: optimistic 409s on text writes, @doc-comment markers, and current.json publishing the reader's position so 'this page' resolves. This is a collaboration design, not an API surface.

The MCP 2026-07-28 angle: the protocol went stateless (no initialize handshake, no session id, no SSE resumability) and open-doc's endpoint was built to that shape — use it to explain the revision in concrete terms rather than abstract ones.
Skills shipped in the scaffolder as the new distribution channel: /create-doc asking four scoping questions and refusing to invent numbers is prompt engineering treated as versioned source.

Honest adoption audit: 78 stars, 1 human contributor, 487 downloads/month, download decay from 459 in launch week to 23, marketing page three versions stale. The ideas are ahead of the traction — say so.

The missing output format is a review-process problem, not a technical one: no .docx means no track changes and no Word comments, which disqualifies open-doc from any organisation whose sign-off runs in Word (issue #35).
Where it fits in a real pipeline: MarkItDown-style ingestion -> agent reasoning -> open-doc production, and why 'agent documents' is two problems that different projects solve.

The local-MCP security shape: loopback Host/Origin validation blocks DNS rebinding but nothing authenticates the caller — and the open allowedHosts bug means the intended escape hatch is broken today.

When to choose it: recurring human-reviewed printable reports authored by a coding agent in an existing React/TypeScript shop. When not to: high-volume server-side PDF generation (react-pdf), markup-first scientific publishing (Pandoc/Quarto/Typst), or anything that must end as .docx.

H2: The problem it names correctly — agents write well and format terribly

faq.a: An MIT-licensed React-first document framework (@open-document/core) in which a coding agent writes each report as React components while the framework supplies real A4/B4/A3 page geometry, a self-filling table of contents, running page numbers, DOM-measured auto-pagination, layout diagnostics and PDF/HTML/PNG/SVG export. Scaffold with `npx @open-document/cli init my-docs`, then run `open-doc dev` for the studio on port 5273.

faq.q: How is it different from react-pdf?
faq.a: Different bet and different scale. @react-pdf/renderer is a renderer with its own layout engine and a PDF component set, used inside applications — 22.5M downloads last month. open-doc is a document workspace for human+agent co-authoring: viewer, inspector, themes, skills, an MCP endpoint, and a layout checker that tells an agent which page overflows and at which line:column. Pick react-pdf for high-volume programmatic PDFs; pick open-doc for printable reports a person steers in chat.

No. It exports PDF, HTML, per-page PNG and SVG. An open issue (#35, filed 2026-09-21) requests .docx precisely because organisations that review in Word need track changes and comments — today a PDF is the end of the line for both.

faq.q: Does it need a browser to make a PDF?
faq.a: Yes, and that is deliberate: PDF export uses the browser print pipeline at the true page size so that what you see is what prints. Headless export (`open-doc export --format pdf`) needs playwright with chromium installed — it is an optional peer dependency, not a bundled one.

faq.q: Can it run headless in CI?
faq.a: Yes. `open-doc check` renders every page at true size, reports clipped content, blank sheets, stranded headings, too-small type and failed images with source locations, and exits non-zero — so the same command that advises an agent can fail a pipeline.

faq.q: Which AI agents can drive it?
faq.a: Anything that writes files or speaks MCP. Skills ship in the scaffolder (/create-doc, /doc-authoring, /current-doc, /apply-comments, /create-theme) for coding agents that read skill directories, and `open-doc dev --mcp` mounts 23 tools at http://localhost:5273/mcp for any MCP client.

faq.q: Is the MCP endpoint safe to expose?
faq.a: Not as shipped. It validates Host and Origin against loopback to block DNS rebinding (403 on both), and authenticates nothing. Beyond loopback you need an authenticating reverse proxy — and note open issue #34: `allowedHosts` from open-doc.config.ts is currently never passed to the MCP plugin, so even an intentionally configured non-loopback host gets a 403 Invalid Host.

A4, JIS B4 (257 x 364 mm) and A3, portrait or landscape — six sheets. Letter, A5 and Legal were removed in 0.4.0 so every document maps onto paper a print shop actually stocks. A4 is laid out at 794 x 1123 px @ 96 dpi with a matching @page descriptor, so nothing rescales at print time.

Very early. Created 2026-08-17, 78 GitHub stars, 7 forks, one human contributor (12 commits), ~487 npm downloads/month for core, and a download curve that decayed from 459 in launch week to 23 in the last full week. The last release was 2026-09-03 (core 0.6.0 / mcp 0.3.2). Treat it as a well-argued design you can read end to end in an afternoon, not a load-bearing dependency.

Conceptually, yes — the same agent-native authoring pattern applied to a different medium, and the README makes the analogy explicit ('If open-slide is Google Slides for agents, open-doc is Google Docs'). open-slide is a separate project (8,587 stars). They are not the same codebase.
